products.description: Epictetus's Enchiridion complete — all fifty-three chapters, 7,299 words — with a selection of the Discourses stated openly: twenty-four of the ninety-five surviving chapters, each complete and uncut, 41,468 words, in P. E. Matheson's English translation of 1916, with Arrian's own Prologue: the founding chapter on things in our power; on progress; on contentment; on constancy before power; the duties hidden in the names we bear; the struggle against impressions; on the faculty of expression; on adornment; and the great close of Book IV — on freedom, on freedom from fear, and on attention. The remaining seventy-one chapters are not reprinted, as the book's Note on the Text states plainly. Original introduction, a note on the text naming the selection, a short life of Epictetus with chronology, a short note before the Enchiridion and before each Discourses book group, a glossary of Stoic terms, and a reading guide by editor Dima Grossman. products.description: Xenophon's Memorabilia complete — all four books, all thirty-nine chapters, 58,402 words — in H. G. Dakyns's English translation of 1897: the defence against the charges of impiety and corrupting the young; the argument from design; self-control as the foundation of virtue; the Choice of Heracles; what a friend is worth and how to choose one; the would-be general and the would-be statesman; the painter and the sculptor on whether art can show the soul; the examination of Euthydemus; and the last days of Socrates, ready to die. Dakyns's own footnotes and his Analysis are not reprinted, as the book's Note on the Text states plainly; the companion works of his part-volume — the Apology, the Economist, the Symposium, and the Hiero — are separate works and are not in this book. products.description: Aristotle's Politics complete — all eight books, all one hundred and three chapters, 87,707 words — in Benjamin Jowett's English translation (Clarendon Press, 1885; revised 1908): the city by nature and man the political animal; the household, slavery, and the art of acquisition; the answer to Plato's Republic; Sparta, Crete, and Carthage examined; the citizen and the classification of constitutions; the middle class and the best state possible; the anatomy of revolution; how tyrannies are preserved; and the best state itself, with its education for leisure. products.title: Lives of the Eminent Philosophers: A Selection (Annotated)
products.creator: Diogenes Laërtius
products.excerpt: The ancient world's biographer of philosophy — eight lives complete and uncut: Thales, Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, Diogenes the Cynic, Zeno, Pyrrho, and Epicurus, in Hicks's Loeb translation, with a note before each life, a glossary, and a reading guide by Dima Grossman.
products.description: A selection, stated openly: eight lives complete and uncut from Diogenes Laërtius's Lives of the Eminent Philosophers — 82,400 words — in R. D. Hicks's English translation (Loeb Classical Library, 1925): Thales, who predicted the eclipse and cornered the olive presses; Socrates, the dossier behind Plato's drama, hemlock and all; Plato, with his will quoted entire; Aristotle, with his will and the catalogue of his writings; Diogenes the Cynic, who told Alexander to stand out of his light; Zeno of Citium, whose life carries the fullest surviving summary of Stoic doctrine; Pyrrho, who suspended judgement about everything and lived to ninety; and Epicurus, closed with documents, not rumours — his three letters and his forty Principal Doctrines, which survive nowhere else. The remaining lives of the ten books are not reprinted, and Hicks's introduction and footnotes are not reprinted, as the book's Note on the Text states plainly. Original introduction, a note on the text, a short life of Diogenes Laërtius, a short note before each life, a glossary, and a reading guide by editor Dima Grossman. products.title: The Gallic War (Annotated)
products.creator: Julius Caesar
products.excerpt: “Gaul is a whole divided into three parts” — the conqueror's own account of the conquest of Gaul, complete in eight books (the eighth by his officer Aulus Hirtius, printed openly as his), in H. J. Edwards's 1917 Loeb translation, with a note before each book, a glossary, and a reading guide by Dima Grossman.
products.description: Caesar's Gallic War complete — all eight books, 403 chapters, some 84,000 words — in H. J. Edwards's translation (Loeb Classical Library, 1917): the Helvetii on the march and the German king Ariovistus; the Belgae and the near-disaster of the Sambre; the sea-fight against the Veneti; a bridge over the Rhine built in ten days; two descents on Britain; the ethnography of the Gauls, the Germans and the Britons, Druids and all; and the great national revolt of Vercingetorix, ending in the double siege-works of Alesia. Book VIII is by Aulus Hirtius, Caesar's officer, who completed the work after Caesar's death; it is printed openly as his, with his preface, and ends as the manuscripts hand it down — in mid-sentence, on the edge of the civil war. Edwards's introduction and apparatus are not reprinted, as the book's Note on the Text states plainly. Original introduction, a note on the text, a short life of Caesar with chronology, a short note before each book, a glossary, and a reading guide by editor Dima Grossman. Volume 32 opens the Roman shelf: history, after the philosophy shelf — Suetonius and Tacitus follow. Ebook $2.99; paperback $11.99 on Lulu. Blacksmith & Witches Classics, Volume 32.

products.title: Utilitarianism (Annotated)
products.creator: John Stuart Mill
products.excerpt: “It is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied; better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied.” — Mill's Utilitarianism complete in five chapters, with his own four footnotes, an introduction, a note before each chapter, a short life, a glossary, and a reading guide by Dima Grossman.
products.description: John Stuart Mill's Utilitarianism complete in five chapters — the greatest-happiness principle stated by its author: what utilitarianism is (and the answer to the “doctrine worthy only of swine” — better Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied), the ultimate sanction of the principle of utility, the sort of proof it admits, and the connexion between justice and utility — in the text of the seventh edition (1879), with Mill's own four footnotes set as chapter endnotes. Original introduction, a note on the text, a short life of Mill with chronology, a note before each chapter, a glossary of his terms, and a reading guide by editor Dima Grossman. This volume is the companion to On Liberty (Volume 18) and closes the Expansion-2 run of the Classics shelf. Ebook $2.99; paperback $11.99 on Lulu. Blacksmith & Witches Classics, Volume 36.

products.title: The Twelve Caesars (Annotated)
products.creator: Suetonius
products.excerpt: “Since well I've played my part, all clap your hands” — Augustus's deathbed, in the dossier of the twelve Caesars filed by their own secretary: all twelve lives complete, in J. C. Rolfe's Loeb translation (1913–14), with a note before each life, a glossary, and a reading guide by Dima Grossman.
products.description: Suetonius's Lives of the Caesars complete — all twelve lives, 541 chapters, some 124,000 words — in J. C. Rolfe's translation (Loeb Classical Library, Vol. I 1913, Vol. II 1914): Augustus's private letters, his will and his deathbed request for applause; Tiberius on his rock at Capri; Caligula conversing with the moon and promising his horse a consulship; Claudius found trembling behind a curtain and made emperor; Nero's last performance; the year of the four emperors; Vespasian joking “Dear me, I think I am becoming a god”; Domitian alone, stabbing flies. The one wound of the transmitted text is stated openly: the opening of the Julius is lost, and the life begins, as the manuscripts give it, in Caesar's sixteenth year. Rolfe's introduction and apparatus are not reprinted, as the book's Note on the Text states plainly. Original introduction, a note on the text, a short life of Suetonius with chronology, a short note before each life, a glossary, and a reading guide by editor Dima Grossman. Volume 33 is the second volume of the Roman shelf opened by Caesar's Gallic War (Volume 32); Tacitus follows. Ebook $2.99; paperback $19.99 on Lulu. Blacksmith & Witches Classics, Volume 33.

products.title: The Annals (Annotated)
products.creator: Tacitus
products.excerpt: “Without either bitterness or partiality” — Tacitus's promise, and the coldest history ever written: the Annals as transmitted — Tiberius, Germanicus, Sejanus, Nero — in Church & Brodribb's translation (Macmillan, 1876), with a note before each book, a glossary, and a reading guide by Dima Grossman.
products.description: Tacitus's Annals as transmitted — Books I–VI and XI–XVI, 721 chapters, some 158,000 words — in A. J. Church and W. J. Brodribb's translation (Macmillan, 1876): the death of Augustus and Tiberius's accession, the mutinies and Germanicus, the treason trials and Sejanus, Tiberius on Capri and his five-period obituary, Messalina's fall, Agrippina and the poisoning of Claudius, Nero, the fire of Rome, Seneca's death, and Thrasea Paetus, where the text breaks off. The losses of the tradition are stated openly and nowhere filled: Books VII–X lost entire, Book V mutilated (the fall of Sejanus falls in the gap), Book XI opening mid-sentence, Book XVI breaking off mid-sentence. The translators' introduction and notes are not reprinted, as the book's Note on the Text states plainly. Original introduction, a note on the text, a short life of Tacitus with chronology, a short note before each book, a glossary, and a reading guide by editor Dima Grossman. Volume 34 closes the Roman shelf opened by Caesar's Gallic War (Volume 32) and Suetonius's Twelve Caesars (Volume 33). Ebook $2.99; paperback $19.99 on Lulu.
